**What the Mirror Kept**

The vaccine was supposed to end it. That was the promise: one dose, and no more winters spent counting the dead.

Instead, within six weeks, it emptied the world. The lucky ones died quietly in their sleep. The rest went insane, whispering to people nobody else could see until their bodies gave out. My husband, Tomas, spent his last four days sitting in the dark bathroom, apologizing to the mirror.

I should have followed him. I'd taken the same dose, in the same clinic, on the same Tuesday. But on day forty I woke with a clear head and an apartment that still smelled like him.

I avoided mirrors. I hung a bedsheet over the bathroom one and kept the rest of the apartment dark. In the abandoned houses I scavenged, I'd found the insane curled up in front of mirrors, palms flat against the glass, as if trying to climb in.

A week later I ran out of excuses. I pulled down the sheet and looked.

The woman in the mirror had my hair, my chipped tooth, my scar through the left eyebrow. But one of her eyes, brown all my life, had turned gray. Tomas's gray.

I stepped closer, and the rest surfaced like watermarks. My mother's stubborn jaw. My brother's freckles. The crooked half smile Tomas wore whenever he was about to apologize. Everyone I had lost was in my face, layered there, faint and patient, looking back.

That was when I understood. The vaccine hadn't poisoned anyone. It had made room for everyone we'd ever lost, and the ones who died and the ones who screamed had simply been unable to look.

I looked until I could bear it. Then I looked a little longer.

"Hello," I whispered.

Every one of them smiled back.

Networks embedded on surfaces arise in applications ranging from transport and communication design to terrain analysis and geometric modeling. Computing optimal or canonical networks on a surface is difficult because topological constraints, such as genus, boundary components and homotopy classes, interact with geometric ones. We introduce a framework that handles these constraints by passing to general covering spaces of the surface, in which the relevant structure is simpler to represent and manipulate. Networks on the base surface are lifted to the cover, optimized there under a symmetry condition, and projected back, so that questions about the surface reduce to questions about a more tractable space. We show that this correspondence preserves length and connectivity, characterize the covers that are sufficient for a given class of networks, and derive bounds on the size of the cover required. As applications, we obtain algorithms for computing shortest and Steiner-type networks within prescribed homotopy classes, and we describe how the same machinery extends to networks with branching and boundary conditions. Our approach recasts several previously separate constructions as instances of one covering-space principle.

**From Teenage Curiosity to a Visit From the FBI**

When Timothy Winslow was a teenager, most of his free time went to one thing: exploring computer systems. He wasn't interested in sports or in the usual hangouts. What drew him in was the challenge of finding out how networked machines worked, and he pursued it across the country, connecting to systems at companies, universities and institutions he had never visited.

To Winslow, it felt like curiosity. He says he never thought of it as crime. He was learning how the systems fit together, tracing connections from one machine to another and seeing how far a single login could take him. "It was like a giant map that nobody had finished drawing," he recalled.

Then the FBI arrived.

The agents' visit turned what he saw as a hobby into a serious legal matter. Federal law treats unauthorized access to computer systems as a crime regardless of the intent behind it, and investigators had no way to know whether a curious teenager was also a threat. For a young person who had spent months immersed in a world of terminals and passwords, the experience was a sudden reminder that the real world has rules his curiosity had ignored.

Cases like Winslow's are not unusual. As computers became central to business and government, a generation of young enthusiasts taught themselves how to move through networks, often without understanding the consequences. Some were prosecuted. Others were warned. A few were later hired by the same organizations they had probed.

Security experts say the story illustrates a persistent tension. The same skills that can be used to break into systems are the ones needed to defend them, and many of today's professionals started out exactly as Winslow did. What separates a career from a criminal record, they argue, often comes down to permission, guidance and timing.

Winslow says he doesn't regret what he learned. He does, however, wish someone had told him earlier where the line was. "I would have been glad to explore the right way," he said, "if I'd known there was one."

Practical Skills or Theory at University?

Many people ask what a university should teach. Some people think students must learn practical job skills. Other people think theory is more important. I think both ideas have good points.

First, practical skills are very useful. When students finish university, they need to find a job. Companies often want workers who can do the work immediately. For example, a student who studies computer science should know how to write real programs, not only read about them. Also, practical classes like internships give students experience. They can meet people in the company and learn how an office works. This makes it easier to get the first job.

However, theoretical knowledge is important too. Theory teaches students how to think. When you understand why something works, you can solve new problems by yourself. Technology changes very fast. A skill that is popular today can be old in five years. But if a student understand the basic ideas, he or she can learn new tools quickly. For example, a person who knows the theory of economics can understand many different jobs in business, and not only one.

Another point is that university is not only for getting a job. It is a place to grow up, to ask big questions and to learn about the world. If a university only teaches job skills, students may lose this chance.

In my opinion, the best universities should mix both. Students need theory in the first years to build a strong base. After that, they should do projects, practice and internships so they can use what they learned. In this way, they will be ready for work and also be able to keep learning in the future.

To sum up, practical skills help students get a job, and theory helps them have a good career for a long time. I believe a balance is the best answer.

# Boko Haram Reportedly Pledges Allegiance to ISIS

Nigerian militant group Boko Haram has reportedly pledged its allegiance to ISIS, a move that could link two of the world's most feared extremist organizations, though experts say the immediate effect on the ground may be limited.

The reported pledge would mark a significant step for Boko Haram, which has carried out bombings, kidnappings and mass killings in northeastern Nigeria and neighboring countries for years. The group is best known internationally for the abduction of hundreds of schoolgirls from the town of Chibok. By aligning itself with ISIS, which controls territory in Syria and Iraq, Boko Haram appears to be seeking greater prominence within the global jihadist movement.

Analysts note that such declarations often carry as much symbolic weight as operational meaning. Peter Pham, an expert on African security issues, said the merger is unlikely to alter the military situation in the short term.

"In the short term, the merger won't have a big impact on the battlefield," Pham said, suggesting that the practical challenges of coordinating across thousands of miles will limit any immediate effect. Boko Haram and ISIS operate in very different environments, and neither group is believed to be in a position to send large numbers of fighters or substantial resources to the other quickly.

Even so, observers say the pledge could have longer-term consequences. An association with ISIS may help Boko Haram with recruitment and propaganda, and it could open the door to more sharing of tactics, training and funding over time. It may also encourage regional governments and international partners to treat the threat as part of a broader fight against ISIS.

The Nigerian government and its neighbors have been working to push back against Boko Haram, but the group has continued to carry out deadly attacks. Officials have not yet commented in detail on the reported pledge, and it is not clear how ISIS will respond to the declaration.

The claim "four out of five dentists recommend" is a marketing statement, and its meaning depends on how the underlying survey was conducted. Companies do sometimes survey dentists, but the sample is often small, and the question is frequently phrased loosely. Respondents may be asked whether they would recommend a product, or they may be allowed to name several brands, which means that many brands can each claim to be endorsed by most dentists. The figure therefore does not necessarily indicate that 80 percent of dentists prefer that toothpaste above all others. Consumers should look for the sample size, the exact wording of the question, and evidence of independent approval, such as the seal of a recognized dental association.

We study kinetic theory models for the distribution of wealth in a market economy, with particular attention to the emergence of power-law tails. Within a Boltzmann-type framework, agents exchange wealth through binary trades that combine a conservative component with a stochastic one representing risk and speculation. Starting from the resulting master equation, we derive Fokker-Planck-type approximations in the limit of small exchanges and obtain stationary distributions in closed form. We show that when agents are partitioned into groups with different saving propensities or different degrees of risk, each group relaxes to an exponential or gamma-type equilibrium with its own characteristic scale. The distribution of wealth over the whole population is then a superposition of these exponentials. We demonstrate analytically that such an overlap, weighted by a suitable distribution of scales, generates a Pareto power-law tail with an exponent determined by the statistics of the parameters. Numerical simulations of the underlying particle system confirm the analytical predictions and show convergence toward the stationary profiles. The results offer a transparent mechanism by which heterogeneity among economic agents produces the heavy-tailed wealth distributions observed in empirical data, and they clarify the conditions under which the bulk and the tail of the distribution coexist.

The lights didn't go out. That was what Teodora kept explaining to the people who panicked in the first hour. It was not darkness, it was nothing, the absence of a thing you did not know could be absent.

She had been blind since age six. At forty-one, she had her routine memorized the way other people remember song lyrics: eleven steps from the bed to the door, the third stair that creaked, the corner where the bus shelter smelled of rain and diesel. When the world went blind at 8:14 on a Tuesday morning, she was already at the shelter, and she heard the screaming begin.

It started with a car horn that didn't stop. Then glass. Then, across the street, a woman's voice repeating "I can't see, I can't see" like a prayer she'd forgotten the end of.

Teodora stood up. She was not afraid, and it surprised her how little she needed to think about it.

"Over here," she called, in her clear teacher's voice. "Follow my voice. Put your hand on the wall."

Within an hour, forty people had gathered in the shelter and the pharmacy beside it. By evening, there were two hundred. They came because she was one of the few people in the city who knew how to move.

Within a week, nobody asked whether she should lead.

The sighted had lost everything at once. They bumped into doorframes and scalded themselves on stoves. They did not know that you can tell a room's size by its echo, or that a cane swept in a slow arc finds the curb before the curb finds you. Teodora and the others from the old Braille club, from the school on Alder Street, from the long quiet years of practice, became teachers by necessity. They taught people to count steps, to label cans with rubber bands, to listen.

The city reorganized itself around them. Rope lines ran along main streets, knotted at intersections in patterns anyone could learn by touch. Ration lines formed according to voice and rhythm. Marcus, who had been blind from birth and had once been laughed at in job interviews, ran the food distribution from memory because he could hold forty names and quantities in his head without writing anything down.

Yet Teodora noticed something that troubled her. Some of the blind who had once been ignored began to enjoy the reversal a little too much. In the third week, a man named Ferris, newly sighted-turned-blind, reached for a ration and was turned away with a laugh. "Now you know," someone told him. He stood there with his hand out.

Teodora walked over that night and found him sitting on the curb, crying quietly.

"You're angry," she said. "It's okay. I was angry for years."

"I just want it to be over," he whispered.

"It might not be." She sat beside him. "But I'll tell you what no one told me when I was six. It gets quieter. And then you start to hear things."

He was silent for a long time. Then he said, "What do you hear?"

"Right now? A woman humming two streets over. Someone fixing a pipe. A child laughing, who still thinks this is a game."

Ferris turned his face toward the sounds.

"Teach me," he said.

She took his hand, laid it on the rope line, and began.

Space Exploration or Problems on Earth?

Many people ask if governments should spend money on space exploration. Some people think this money should be used to solve problems on Earth, like hunger, sickness and poverty. I think both sides have good points, but I believe governments should spend a small part of their money on space, and most of it on problems here.

First, I understand why people are against space spending. Every day, many people in the world do not have enough food or clean water. Hospitals in poor countries often does not have enough doctors or medicine. When I see this, it is hard to say that sending a rocket to Mars is more important. Rockets are very expensive, and one launch can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. This money could build many schools or clinics.

However, space exploration also gives us many benefits. For example, scientists who work on space projects invented many things we use every day. Satellites give us weather information, so farmers can know when it will rain and people can get ready for big storms. GPS in our phones also comes from space technology. Some medical tools were also developed from research for astronauts. So the money is not really lost in the sky. It comes back to Earth in another form.

Also, space research can teach us about our own planet. By looking at Earth from space, scientists can see how the climate is changing and how forests are getting smaller. This information help governments make better decisions. In the future, space may even give us new resources or a new place to live if Earth has big problems.

Another point is that space projects give many people jobs. Engineers, scientists, builders and teachers all work on them. Young people become interested in science because they dream about being astronauts. This is good for the future of a country.

Still, I think governments must be careful. The space budget is usually only a small part of all government spending, so it is not the main reason why problems on Earth are not solved. But if a country has many people without homes or food, solving those problems should come first. A good government should look after its people before it looks at the stars.

In conclusion, I think space exploration is useful and we should not stop it completely. But governments should spend most of their money on problems on Earth, and keep space spending small and smart. In this way, we can take care of today and also prepare for tomorrow.
